articles.title: DHS’ 4-year cap on student visa stays struck down by federal judge
articles.summary: A federal judge struck down the Department of Homeland Security’s four-year cap on student visa stays. The judge ruled that the law does not grant DHS broad and open-ended authority to undermine the student visa program.
articles.insight:
This ruling temporarily removes a restrictive U.S. visa policy, potentially improving perceived stability and long-term study prospects for international students—though actual demand shifts will depend on broader factors like tuition costs, post-study work rights, and geopolitical sentiment across key source markets.  
Admissions teams should track U.S. government appeals or new regulatory proposals, while benchmarking how peer institutions in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand position their own visa pathways and graduate outcomes to maintain competitive appeal.

articles.title: Canada announces targets for new international student arrivals through 2029
articles.summary: The Canadian government has announced temporary immigration targets for 2027, 2028, and 2029 as part of the 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan, released on 5 November alongside the federal budget. The plan sets an annual cap of 370,000 study permits for new international student arrivals during those years.
articles.insight:
Canada’s 370,000-per-year cap on new study permits signals a deliberate move to stabilize international student numbers after recent growth and scrutiny, potentially shifting demand toward alternative destinations—but actual enrolment shifts depend on how strictly the cap is enforced and whether it affects perceived quality or post-study work prospects.  
Admissions teams should track Canadian visa processing times, provincial policy adjustments, and real-time source-market sentiment—especially among high-potential applicants from India, Nigeria, and the Philippines—to assess whether this cap meaningfully alters competitive positioning in key recruitment corridors.

articles.title: US court strikes down rule that would have ended Duration of Status (D/S) for international students
articles.summary: On 16 November 2026, a U.S. federal judge in the District of Massachusetts struck down the Department of Homeland Security’s final rule that would have eliminated the Duration of Status (D/S) policy for international students, exchange visitors, and foreign media representatives. The court ruled the regulation was “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedure Act.
articles.insight:
This ruling preserves the current D/S framework for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders, potentially sustaining enrolment stability for U.S. institutions—though its direct impact on global demand remains uncertain given broader geopolitical, economic, and reputational factors influencing student choices.  
Admissions teams should monitor U.S. DHS appeals activity, policy developments in other destination countries responding to this decision, and source-market sentiment shifts—particularly among Asian and Latin American prospects weighing U.S. visa predictability against alternatives like the UK’s Graduate Route or Australia’s post-study work reforms.

articles.title: Campus France recebe inscrições para brasileiros estudarem na França em 2027
articles.summary: Campus France is currently accepting applications from Brazilian students who wish to pursue undergraduate or master’s degree programs in France starting in 2027. The announcement was published on November 18, 2026, at 6:00 a.m.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential shifts in Brazilian student preferences toward European destinations, possibly reflecting evolving perceptions of affordability, post-study work opportunities, or geopolitical factors—though it remains unclear whether this represents a structural trend or short-term response to specific policy changes in France or competing countries.  
Admissions teams should monitor Brazilian application volumes and enrolment trends over the next 12–18 months, particularly for undergraduate and master’s programs, while reviewing their value propositions on cost, career outcomes, and visa pathways relative to France’s updated offerings.

articles.title: NMC proposes easing licensing rules for foreign medical graduates; DGHS approves stipend parity at five institutes
articles.summary: The National Medical Commission has proposed draft amendment regulations for 2026 to ease licensing requirements for Foreign Medical Graduates by replacing the current eligibility condition with registration under the professional regulatory body in the country where their medical degree was awarded, and has invited public suggestions and objections. Separately, the Directorate General of Health Services has approved stipend parity for Foreign Medical Graduate interns with Indian medical graduates at five government medical institutions.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential softening of India’s domestic medical education barriers for students who trained abroad, which could modestly reduce outbound demand for postgraduate clinical training—though undergraduate and non-clinical health programs remain largely unaffected and visa pathways to Western countries remain attractive.  
Admissions teams should monitor NMC’s final 2026 regulations and stipend implementation timelines across the five institutes, as sustained policy execution may gradually influence perceptions of return-on-investment for Indian students pursuing overseas MBBS degrees.

articles.title: Record £400m Erasmus+ funding opens international opportunities for UK
articles.summary: Applications have opened for a record £400 million in Erasmus+ funding for the UK. More than 100,000 people across the UK are expected to benefit from international education, training, and development opportunities through this funding.
articles.insight:
This £400m Erasmus+ funding boost signals renewed UK government commitment to international mobility, potentially reinforcing perceptions of the UK as an accessible, globally connected study destination—though its direct impact on non-EU undergraduate demand remains uncertain amid broader visa and post-study work policy shifts.  
Admissions teams should monitor uptake patterns among UK-based Erasmus+ participants (e.g., short-term exchanges, staff mobility) for early indicators of strengthened institutional partnerships or shifting student preferences, while cross-referencing with Home Office visa statistics and source-market sentiment surveys over the next 6–12 months.

articles.title: Decline in number of Indian students studying in U.S.
articles.summary: The number of Indian students studying in the United States has declined. Nevertheless, India remains the top sending country for international students to the U.S.
articles.insight:
The decline in Indian students enrolling in U.S. institutions may reflect shifting preferences due to evolving visa policies, rising costs, or stronger domestic and regional alternatives—but it does not yet indicate a broad erosion of India’s strong outbound education demand.  
Admissions teams should monitor Indian student application trends across destinations, track policy developments like U.S. H-1B reforms or UK post-study work extensions, and assess how competitor nations’ marketing and support services are resonating with key Indian segments.

articles.title: 200k UK-EU youth mobility places agreed as tuition fee decision delayed
articles.summary: The UK and EU have agreed on a youth mobility scheme providing 100,000 places for young people from each side to live, work, and study in the other region for up to three years, totaling 200,000 places. A decision on university tuition fees for participants in the scheme has been delayed by six months.
articles.insight:
This agreement signals potential shifts in European and UK youth mobility preferences, possibly dampening short-term demand for traditional degree pathways among 18–30-year-olds—though its direct impact on international undergraduate or postgraduate enrolments remains uncertain amid broader geopolitical and economic factors.  
Admissions teams should monitor uptake of the scheme’s work-and-study placements, especially among EU nationals considering UK institutions, and assess whether delayed tuition fee clarity affects application timing or choice patterns relative to competing destinations like Canada or Australia.

articles.title: Vietnam no longer Japan's largest source of visa overstayers as violations drop
articles.summary: Thais have become the largest group of visa overstayers in Japan, surpassing Vietnamese nationals. Vietnamese visa overstayers declined by 12.6% in the first half of the year.
articles.insight:
This news hints at shifting migration patterns and potential softening of Vietnam’s outbound student demand due to tightening visa compliance awareness, though it doesn’t directly indicate reduced enrolment intent—many overstayers are not students, and educational visa pathways remain distinct from work-based overstaying.  
Admissions teams should monitor Vietnamese student application volumes, visa refusal rates, and agent sentiment over the next 12–18 months, while also benchmarking against Thailand’s evolving student mobility trends to assess possible regional policy spillovers or competitive repositioning opportunities.
